query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A synchronized ultrafast in‐situ synchrotron X‐ray diffraction coupled with fast scanning calorimetry can simultaneously capture the liquid‐state structure and thermal signals during melting of high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) so as to determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties with improved accuracy. In particular, the approach will reveal that the vibrational contributions and nonideal mixing in the liquid state (which are not well captured by conventional DSC or slow scanning techniques) scale systematically with the degree of compositional complexity across the HEA family.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogeneous, single‐phase as‐cast high‐entropy alloys (e.g., both refractory and noble HEAs with equiatomic or near‐equiatomic compositions)
generation.intervention: Perform controlled rapid heating (and subsequent cooling) experiments while simultaneously collecting ultrafast X‐ray diffraction patterns and calorimetric heat flow data using a synchronized, high‐throughput experimental setup.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted in a controlled atmosphere over a temperature range from room temperature to well above melting (with heating increments fast enough to preserve transient liquid-state signals, yet slow enough for sufficient relaxation) and using a heating rate calibrated to capture rapid structural rearrangements.
generation.structural_mediator: Real‐time liquid‐phase atomic arrangements and associated volume changes measured directly by high-speed diffraction that mediate the interpretation of thermal events recorded by calorimetry.
generation.mechanism: When the HEA is heated, the onset of melting is characterized by an abrupt change in diffraction peak positions (indicating volume expansion and loss of long-range order) together with endothermic signals in the calorimetry. The simultaneous capture allows deconvolution of the vibrational component of the entropy and the nonideal mixing effects in the liquid state, thus linking structural fluctuations with thermodynamic quantities.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated method will determine melting temperatures within ±2% of expected values from post-mortem analysis, quantify fusion enthalpy and entropy within experimental uncertainty (±5%), and measure liquid-phase volume changes accurately. Moreover, a systematic variation in the vibrational/free energy contributions with increasing configurational complexity is expected.
generation.baseline: Traditional separate DSC measurements, post-mortem XRD, and conventional MD simulations or CALPHAD predictions.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to work reliably for single-phase HEAs that do not exhibit severe liquid immiscibility or multiple overlapping phase transitions; extreme cases with very high component counts might challenge the signal contrast or require further calibration of the technique.
generation.uncertainty: While MD simulations of refractory HEAs (e.g., PMC8956691 evidence on MD‐based melting behavior) and studies on rare earth oxides (PMC7412006 evidence on volume and nonideal mixing effects) support the rational design of this approach, uncertainties remain regarding the synchronization of ultrafast measurements and calibration across different HEA compositions. The practical implementation in diverse chemical spaces remains to be fully demonstrated.

cited_evidence.text: Calphad [,,,] modeling was performed to compare with experimental results. Calphad-type thermodynamic database for rare earth sesquioxides was created by Zinkevich []. He critically reviewed all relevant experimental data available before 2006 and evaluated missing fusion enthalpies values based on measured enthalpy of fusion and volume change on melting for Y2O3. In a more recent evaluation by Zhang and Jung [] evaluation, missing data were estimated from liquidus in RE2O3-Al2O3 phase diagrams. However, new measurements for fusion enthalpies [] are in better agreement with Zinkevich’s assessment. Zhang and Jung’s evaluation varies largely with the values proposed by Konings et al. []. Zinkevich [] database for rare earth sesquioxides is openly available at the NIST website [] and was used in this work without any modifications. Thermo-Calc (Stockholm, Sweden) software was used for calculations.

The melting mechanism of single crystal and polycrystalline Nb20.6Mo21.7Ta15.6W21.1V21.0 refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) were investigated by the molecular dynamics (MD) simulation using the second-nearest neighbor modified embedded-atom method (2NN MEAM) potential. For the single crystal RHEA, the density profile displays an abrupt drop from 11.25 to 11.00 g/cm3 at temperatures from 2910 to 2940 K, indicating all atoms begin significant local structural rearrangement. For polycrystalline RHEAs, a two-stage melting process is found. In the first melting stage, the melting of the grain boundary (GB) regions firstly occurs at the pre-melting temperature, which is relatively lower than the corresponding system-melting point. At the pre-melting temperature, most GB atoms have enough kinetic energies to leave their equilibrium positions, and then gradually induce the rearrangement of grain atoms close to GB. In the second melting stage at the melting point, most grain atoms have enough kinetic energies to rearrange, resulting in the chemical short-ranged order changes of all pairs.
